To revolve or rotate around a centre.

examples.text: The body was turning round slowly as it fell.

glosses: To turn so as to be facing in the opposite direction.

examples.text: It seemed that there was someone behind me; but when I turned round, no one was there.

glosses: To change one's opinion or attitude (especially when becoming hostile etc.).

examples.text: You can't turn round and blame me all of a sudden.

glosses: To make revolve, rotate.
To put into an opposing position; to reverse.

examples.text: He turned the glass round and examined the other side.

glosses: To make (a ship, airplane etc.) ready for departure.

examples.text: The stopover is very short, and crews will have about 15 minutes to turn the plane round.

The interest of individual ships and merchants frequently clash with the general interest, but at times of pressure there is seldom disagreement on the point that the best arrangements are those which permit the greatest number of vessels to be turned round in any given time.

glosses: To process; to complete work on (something), especially with a view to sending it on in a finished state.

examples.text: New figures are in. We need to turn these round ASAP: the boss wants a report tonight.

glosses: To bring back into a particular place or condition; to restore.
To cause (something) to turn around a central point.
To orbit a central point (especially of a celestial body).

examples.text: The Earth revolves around the sun.

glosses: To rotate around an axis.

examples.text: The Earth revolves once every twenty-four hours.

It is never possible to settle down to the ordinary routine of life at sea until the screw begins to revolve. There is an hour or two, after the passengers have embarked, which is disquieting and fussy.

glosses: To move in order or sequence.

examples.text: The program revolves through all the queues before returning to the start.

glosses: To ponder on; to reflect repeatedly upon; to consider all aspects of.

examples.text: These are the difficulties which arise to me on revolving this scheme […].
He sits silent, revolving many thoughts, at the foot of St. Edmund’s Shrine.

glosses: To read through, to study (a book, author etc.).

examples.text: This having heard, strait I again revolv’d / The Law and Prophets.

glosses: The rotation of part of the scenery within a theatrical production.
The rotating section itself.

examples.text: […] a revolving stage, two-level platforms stage left and stage right, and a large bridge that connected the platforms midstage, twelve feet up off the revolve.

glosses: A radical change; revolution.
A movement where a person spins round elegantly; a pirouette.
Any rotating movement; a spin.

examples.text: The conductor gave his baton a twirl, and the orchestra began to play.

glosses: A little twist of some substance; a swirl.

examples.text: Place the cream in a piping bag with a fairly large star pipe attached, fill each tartlet with a twirl of cream and top with a strawberry.

glosses: A prison guard.

examples.text: Which was in the main childishness and pettiness, the reason for this was that most of the twirls and the governors had […]

glosses: To perform a twirl.
To rotate rapidly.

examples.text: See ruddy maids, / Some taught with dexterous hand to twirl the wheel.
No more beneath soft eve's consenting star / Fandango twirls his jocund castanet.

glosses: To twist round.

examples.text: He inflated his chest, twirled his moustache, and thumped the table with a revulsion to thunderous indignation.

glosses: To pitch.

examples.text: When the batteries were announced, however, and Herb Pennock of the Boston Red Sox, probably the best pitcher in all baseballdom, was named to twirl for the invading team, we felt we had been tricked.

glosses: To linger, loiter, or stay.

examples.text: If you hang about after the show, you can meet the cast.
The stranger kept hanging about just inside the inn door, peering round the corner like a cat waiting for a mouse.
He was taken into the mountain by the fairies, and had been with them for many years, and at last they wanted him to marry their daughter, who was always hanging about after him.

Although unusual in the Dublin area, he knew that it was not by any means unknown for desperadoes who had next to nothing to live on to be abroad waylaying and generally terrorising peaceable pedestrians by placing a pistol at their head in some secluded spot outside the city proper, famished loiterers of the Thames embankment category they might be hanging about there or simply marauders ready to decamp with whatever boodle they could in one fell swoop at a moment's notice, your money or your life, leaving you there to point a moral, gagged and garrotted.

glosses: Especially in the form to hang about with (someone): to spend time or be friends with.

examples.text: My daughter likes to hang about with older kids after school.

glosses: wait a minute; hold on
To cover or enclose (something) by folding and securing a covering entirely around it.

examples.text: He wrapped up the parcel with brown paper.
Let me wrap you up a piece of this pie to take home with you.
After all the fish were wrapped up, into the office we went to make the entry into the record book.

glosses: To conclude or finish completely.

examples.text: Let me wrap up this project before I begin a new one.
I've just been handed a note about your — the need for you to leave, and I'll wrap it up in another couple of minutes here.
Kevin Doyle cut inside and drove a third, Matt Jarvis hammered in a fourth and David Jones lashed in deep into injury time to wrap it up.
And in reality, that show is a perfect example of a show that knew the end was coming, but still couldn't wrap it up in a meaningful way.
After the event has wrapped up, thank everyone for attending and let them know about any future events.
“The DNA evidence wrapped everything up for us,” Ezra continued.

glosses: To summarize or recapitulate.

examples.text: The newscaster wrapped up the day's events.
Conclusion: Story is clearly wrapped up using general concluding statements such as "and they were together again, happy as can be."
If I were to wrap this up in a single bit of advice, it would be this: Don't end each day without doing five things to further your business.
Here are final points to wrap up what you've read in this chapter:

glosses: To put on abundant clothing as protection from the cold; to bundle up.

examples.text: It's a cold, snowy day and I'm going to wrap up thoroughly before I go sledding.
After the bath wrap up well, preferably in woolen garments, until the perspiration ceases.
However well you wrap up, you get cold.
Every year around the world people pull on their woolly jumpers, wrap up in their thickest coats, dig out their heavy snow boots and get ready for their favourite frosty festivals.

glosses: To cocoon; to surround protectively.

examples.text: It is time once again to just let it be; let love wrap you up and take care of you.
Let's just say in the past my family's tried to wrap me up in cotton wool, and that drives me crazy.
I wanted my possessions to cocoon me, wrap me up, and keep me safe from a world that was trying to rip it all away.
He held out his arms, and I went to him and let him wrap me up tight.

glosses: To tie up; to make too busy to respond.

examples.text: And if you haven't seen these things the technicians can absolutely wrap you up in details, and you never find your way out.

With the seconds slipping away and the gap just one point, France went through an 18-phase attack that made little ground but resulted in an attacking scrum on the New Zealand 10m line, only for the hosts to steal the ball back when Aurelien Rougerie was wrapped up.
This left him with the real problem, if he brought it to their attention now they may well wrap him up in red tape while they requested advice from the high command on how to proceed.

glosses: To combine, incorporate or encapsulate into one thing.

examples.text: With all this wrapped up into one compact machine, it's easy to see why the versatile veteran has become a Champion of the Underground!
He wrapped up into Himself those who would voluntarily acclaim Him their Lord.
We can, however, wrap them all up in one word—salvation.
Now, you can take every religion in the world and you can wrap them all up in one big hairy package, and then you can take 'em and ...
Tom has the smooth moves of A.I.’s Gigolo Joe and some of the quizzical cluelessness of Star Trek’s Data, all wrapped up in the classical good looks of, well, Matthew Crawley.

glosses: To hide or cover up.

examples.text: In briefe, all bookes, divinitie except, Are nought but tales of the divels lawes, Poyson wrapt up in sugred words, Mans pride, damnations props, the worlds abuse.
The dishonest tradesman wraps up the thousand sins of his daily avaricious life, in the bland smile, the cringing bow, and the false statement which he makes to his customers.

This he unquestionably did not do, and yet we are asked to give a hearing to an American lawyer, who, nearly three centuries after Bacon's death, chooses first to imagine that Bacon wrote the immortal plays, and then to assure us that, instead of placing the fact upon record, as any man of common-sense would be sure to place it, he wrapt up his secret in a cryptogram, of which he did not even leave the key — a cryptogram distributed in a most mystical and bewildering way through the bad printing of the first folio, and which it was left for Mr. Donnelly's laborious and perverted ingenuity to discover!
So, we wrap up our secrets and lock them away before swallowing the key, hoping no one finds them.

glosses: To curl into a more compact form.

examples.text: Whereas most people open their front doors to find a nicely wrapped newspaper in the morning, Felix found a sleeping armadillo wrapped up into a protective ball.
Mother Elizabeth, her long hair wrapped up into a crowning bundle on her head, glanced up at them sharply from her seat before the restless group.
These guys all backed off and we were just getting settled back in when suddenly I was getting my arms wrapped up behind me, like I was being arrested.
